newsitem.title: USA: Wisconsin managing school funding plan well - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Wisconsin managing school funding plan well - S&P.

text.p: Increased state funding of school districts in Wisconsin should not adversely impact school financial performance or credit quality, Standard & Poor's Corp. said Monday in its CreditWeek Municipal publication.
Wisconsin's plan to increase state funding of schools to 66 percent from 50 percent took effect during the current fiscal year, which began July 1.
In exchange for greater state financial support, average school property tax rates are expected to decline by about 16.7 percent for the 1996-97 school year, according to Standard & Poor's.

Kenneth Gear, an associate director at Standard & Poor's, said that because state aid also covered a portion of school debt service, districts have had greater success in getting bond referendums passed by voters.

However, the subsequent increase in the state's share of debt service costs has resulted in supplemental state appropriations that have caught the attention of some Wisconsin lawmakers who may address the situation in the future, Gear added.
"If this situation is not addressed, total costs for education could rise faster than previously projected and will place fiscal pressure on the state," the CreditWeek Municipal article stated.
Overall, Standard & Poor's analysts said Wisconsin has been able to handle the greater burden of school funding well.

"They seem to be doing pretty well," said John Fargnoli, a director, adding that the rating agency had had some concerns about the state's reliance on economic growth to raise most of the money for schools.
He added that Standard & Poor's may take action on Wisconsin's rating in the future, but that action would most likely involve the state's rating outlook.
Standard & Poor's rates Wisconsin's general obligation debt AA with a stable outlook.
